summary_html: Findings by **federal/state oversight** (CFSR reviews, OIG audits, child-fatality commissions) can initiate investigations or corrective actions that open CPS involvement. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)). Alabama is not a universal-reporter state: Ala. Code § 26-14-3 sets out who must report, and Ala. Code § 26-14-4 permits any other person to report if they have reasonable cause to suspect a child is being abused or neglected, without requiring it.

key_cases.case_name: R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Walley
key_cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court granted the Commissioner's second motion to terminate the 1991 R.C. consent decree, finding that DHR had met both prongs of the termination clause by achieving and being able to sustain systemwide substantial compliance so that continued judicial oversight was no longer necessary.
key_cases.relevance: The R.C. court monitor's county-by-county reviews are the model for external audit of Alabama's CPS practice.
key_cases.quote: DHR successfully has reformed its child welfare system by developing a system of care which substantially complies with the requirements of the Consent Decree and the Implementation Plan

key_cases.holding: The Court held that although the Alabama Open Records Act carries a presumption in favor of disclosure, FERPA preempts it as to education records, so even redacted student financial-aid forms could not be released.
key_cases.relevance: Oversight bodies seeking agency records in Alabama run into the same federal-preemption limit.
key_cases.quote: Because FERPA prohibits the very release of the redacted financial-aid forms and because FERPA takes precedence over the Open Records Act, the director is entitled to a summary judgment.

key_cases.case_name: R.C. ex rel. Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program v. Nachman
key_cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court denied DHR's Rule 60(b) motion to vacate or modify the 1991 R.C. consent decree, rejecting the claims of collusion, lack of class standing and change of law, finding that DHR came to the court without clean hands and that substantial compliance with the decree's system of care remained a distant goal.
key_cases.relevance: It describes the court monitor's role as the court's agent assessing DHR's compliance county by county, which is the external-oversight machinery Alabama otherwise lacks.
key_cases.quote: The consent decree in this case came about because DHR would not or could not comply with constitutional, federal statutory and common-law mandates.
